info.title: The Drift Problem
info.subtitle: Why two identical oscillators never quite agree, and why we stopped trying to make them

abstract.para: The &vesper; has a knob labelled Drift. It is the most argued-about control we have ever shipped. This issue explains what it does, why the first prototype had none, why the second had far too much, and how we arrived at a model that a room full of engineers could agree sounded alive without sounding broken.

section.title: A sound that was too correct
section.para: The first &vesper; prototype ran on a development board taped to the underside of a plywood panel. Its oscillators were mathematically perfect: a sawtooth at 220 Hz was a sawtooth at exactly 220 Hz, forever, on every voice. We played a six-note chord, and the room went quiet in the wrong way.

Nothing was wrong with it. Every measurement passed. But the chord sat in the speakers like a photograph of a chord. A sound designer on the team described it, with some cruelty, as a spreadsheet that has learned to hum.

What the old instruments we grew up with had, and our prototype lacked, was disagreement. Six voices that each believe they are playing A3 will, on a circuit made of real components, each be a few cents off in a different direction, and the direction will wander. The ear hears that wandering as width, warmth and motion. It is the reason a chord on an old polysynth seems to breathe.

note.title: A cent, briefly
note.para: A cent (¢s;) is one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone. Most listeners cannot pick out a single sustained note that is 5 ¢s; flat, but they can hear two notes 2 ¢s; apart beating against each other as a slow pulse.

section.title: Where real drift comes from
section.para: Before modelling anything, we spent three weeks measuring. We borrowed a dozen instruments from colleagues and friends, warmed them up, and logged their pitch every 50 milliseconds for an hour. Three different behaviours stood out, each with its own time scale.

item.definition: Slow and large. As a circuit warms up, its pitch slides, sometimes by twenty cents over the first quarter of an hour, then settles into a lazy wander of a few cents over minutes.
Static. Two voices built from parts that are each within one per cent of their nominal value will simply not be tuned identically. This never changes; it is a fingerprint.

Fast and tiny. Noise in the power supply and the timing circuitry nudges each cycle a fraction early or late. Alone it is inaudible; it smears the very top of the spectrum just enough to soften a bright sawtooth.

section.para: The important finding was not any one of these, but that they are independent per voice. A single global wobble applied to all six voices, which is what our second prototype did, sounds like a tape machine with a bad motor. It is drift, but it is the wrong drift.

figure.title: One hour of pitch error, voice 3 of a borrowed instrument
figure.description: A line that falls steeply from +18 ¢s; to +3 ¢s; in the first twelve minutes, then wanders between −2 and +5 ¢s; for the remaining forty-eight, with a fine fuzz of jitter along its whole length.

section.title: The second prototype: too much of a good thing
section.para: Our first attempt at modelling drift was a sine-wave LFO, one per instrument, at 0.3 Hz, routed to every oscillator's pitch. Turning it up made the chord swim together, in lockstep, like a choir following a conductor who cannot keep still.

The second attempt gave each voice its own LFO with a random phase. Better, but the periodicity was audible within a few seconds: the ear is extremely good at noticing that something repeats. We had made six seasick metronomes.

The third attempt replaced the LFOs with white noise, low-pass filtered. This is where the trouble really started, because filtered white noise is stationary: it has no memory of where it has been, so it never wanders away. Real drift does. A voice that has drifted sharp tends to stay sharp for a while.

section.title: A bounded random walk
section.para: What finally worked is a random walk with a gentle pull back towards zero, a process statisticians call mean-reverting. Each voice keeps a single number, its current offset in cents. Every control tick, the offset takes a small random step and is then nudged a fraction of the way back towards the centre.
Three properties of this little function matter more than its arithmetic.

item.para: It has memory. Because each step starts from where the last one ended, the offset wanders in long, unhurried arcs instead of fizzing around zero.
It cannot run away. The pull term means that, however long the instrument is left on, the voices stay within a predictable range. The clamp is only there for the knob's extreme end.
It never repeats. There is no period for the ear to latch onto, because there is no oscillator underneath.

note.title: Try it yourself
note.para: Load the factory patch Tidepool Glass, hold a single note, and turn Drift from zero to full over about thirty seconds. Then do the same with a three-note chord. The single note changes very little; the chord comes alive. Drift is a property of relationships between voices, not of any one voice.

section.title: Tolerance: the fingerprint
section.para: The tolerance term in the listing above is fixed when the instrument first boots in the factory. Each voice is assigned a small, permanent offset drawn from a narrow distribution and stored in its calibration memory. Your &vesper;'s voice 4 is slightly flat, and it will be slightly flat for the life of the instrument.
We argued for a long time about whether this was honest. A digital instrument has no real tolerances; we are inventing them. The deciding argument came from a player in our beta group, who wrote:

blockquote.para: I want to know that my instrument is mine. If I sell it and buy another, I want the new one to sound like the same model and not like the same instrument.
blockquote.attribution: A beta tester, in a feedback form

section.para:
So we kept it, and we made it visible. The calibration page in the
Settings
Voices
Character menu shows each voice's fingerprint as a small bar, and it can be reset to a new random fingerprint, or to zero for anyone who wants their &vesper; perfectly matched.

section.title: How much is enough?
section.para: The final question was the range of the knob. We ran a listening test with twenty-four participants, a mixture of players, engineers and people who had never touched a synthesizer. Each heard the same chord progression at eight drift settings in random order and rated it on two scales: alive and out of tune.

table.title: Median ratings by peak drift (1 = not at all, 7 = very)

section.para: The alive curve peaks at four to six cents and falls away after eight, while out of tune climbs steadily. We put four cents at twelve o'clock on the knob and twelve cents at full, so that the centre of the knob is where most people would choose to be, and the extreme is available for anyone who wants it.

note.title: Drift and tuning-critical patches
note.para: Drift is applied before the global tuning stage. If you are playing alongside an acoustic instrument tuned to a fixed reference, set Drift below nine o'clock, or switch on Drift follows tuning so the walk is centred on the reference instead of on zero.

section.title: On the &lantern;
section.para: The &lantern; is a different instrument, built around wavetables and FM, and its voices are meant to sound precise. It still has drift, but it is off by default and its range is a quarter of the &vesper;'s. Applied to an FM operator, even a cent of disagreement between carrier and modulator changes the timbre over time, which is occasionally beautiful and frequently alarming. We left the control in, behind a Character page, for the people who will find the beautiful cases.

section.title: Drift as a modulation source
section.para: On both instruments, each voice's drift value is also exposed as a modulation source, random-per-note, so it can move things other than pitch. Routing it to filter cutoff by a small amount gives each note of a chord a slightly different brightness, which is one of the quietest and most effective tricks in the factory library.

section.title: What we learned
section.para: The lesson of the drift problem is not really about oscillators. It is that correct and right are different targets, and an instrument has to hit the second one. Every measurement we took told us the first prototype was perfect. Every person who played it told us it was not.

The work was to find out what they were hearing, measure that instead, and build the smallest model that reproduced it: one number per voice, a random step, a gentle pull home. Eleven lines of C, three weeks of logging, and a knob people still argue about.
We consider that a success.
